cues.text: Welcome to Chemical Bonding.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Bond formation can lower energy through interactions between nuclei and
electrons.
The octet rule is a useful pattern, not the physical cause of every bond.
Electron deficient species, odd electron species and expanded valence shell
descriptions show its limits.
An ionic solid is an extended lattice, not a collection of isolated pairs held
only by the act of electron transfer.
For comparable structures, greater ionic charges and smaller separations
strengthen electrostatic attraction.
In a Born Haber cycle, add all enthalpy steps with their stated signs.
Lattice formation from gaseous ions releases energy, while separating the
solid
into gaseous ions requires energy; tables may use either convention.
Fajans's rules describe polarization and covalent character.
A small, highly charged cation more strongly distorts a neighbouring electron
cloud.
A large, readily polarizable anion is more easily distorted.
Thus lithium iodide has greater covalent character than lithium fluoride in
the
usual comparison.
The model describes trends, not a sharp boundary dividing every bond into
purely ionic or purely covalent.
A quantitative lattice enthalpy calculation also needs consistent phases,
stoichiometric amounts and all the necessary energy data.
Start a Lewis structure by counting valence electrons from all atoms.
Add electrons for negative charge and subtract for positive charge.
Draw a plausible connected skeleton, fill terminal shells where appropriate,
then place remaining electrons and inspect the central atom.
Carbon dioxide has sixteen valence electrons.
Two carbon oxygen double bonds use eight electrons, and two lone pairs on each
oxygen use the other eight.
Each double bond still counts as one electron domain for shape.
Hydrogen requires a duet, not an octet.
Formal charge equals valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus half
the bonding electrons.
In ammonium, nitrogen has four single bonds and no lone pair.
Five minus zero minus four gives formal charge plus one.
Each hydrogen has formal charge zero, so the total is plus one as required.
Formal charge differs from oxidation number and from an experimentally
inferred
partial charge.
In one carbonate contributor, the double bonded oxygen has formal charge zero
and the two singly bonded oxygens each have minus one, giving the ion's total
minus two.
Every proposed drawing must satisfy both the electron inventory and the net
charge before its stability is compared with alternatives.
Resonance contributors keep atomic positions and connectivity unchanged while
changing electron placement.
They are not separate molecules rapidly switching between drawings.
The actual electronic structure is delocalized and cannot always be
represented
by one localized Lewis structure.
Carbonate has three equivalent contributors, each with one carbon oxygen
double
bond in a different position.
Its three carbon oxygen bonds are equivalent in the ideal symmetric ion.
The simple average Lewis bond order is four thirds, intermediate between a
single and double bond.
In ozone, two equivalent contributors place the double bond on opposite sides,
and the simple average bond order is one point five.
Resonance forms need not always contribute equally.
Equivalent forms have equal weight, while non equivalent contributors differ
in
importance according to features such as octets, charge separation and charge
placement.
Moving an atom or a proton creates a different structural arrangement, not
merely another resonance contributor.
Curved electron arrows begin at an electron pair, not at a positive charge.
Delocalization can affect bond length, stabilization and chemical reactivity.
Use the drawings to explain these consequences rather than interpreting the
resonance arrow as an equilibrium between isolable species.
VSEPR begins with electron domains around the central atom.
A multiple bond counts as one domain, while a lone pair is another domain.
Two domains give a linear arrangement, three trigonal planar, and four
tetrahedral.
Carbon dioxide is linear.
Ammonia has three bond domains and one lone pair: tetrahedral electron
arrangement but trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.
Water has two bonds and two lone pairs and is bent.
Five domains use a trigonal bipyramidal reference arrangement.
In the introductory model, a lone pair prefers an equatorial site because it
encounters fewer ninety degree interactions.
Sulfur tetrafluoride has four bonds and one lone pair and is seesaw shaped.
Chlorine trifluoride has three bonds and two lone pairs and is T shaped.
Xenon difluoride has two bonds and three lone pairs and is linear.
Six domains use an octahedral reference arrangement.
Sulfur hexafluoride is octahedral; xenon tetrafluoride has four bonds and two
opposite lone pairs and is square planar.
These shape rules are useful models.
Exact bond angles and lengths depend on the species, and a shape name alone
does not prove a literal d orbital hybridization mechanism in hypervalent
bonding.
A polar bond does not automatically make the entire molecule polar.
Bond dipoles must be combined with directions and molecular geometry.
Carbon dioxide has polar carbon oxygen bonds, but in the ideal linear molecule
the equal opposite contributions cancel.
Bent water does not have this cancellation.
Trigonal planar boron trifluoride and tetrahedral carbon tetrachloride are
other familiar symmetric examples with zero net permanent molecular dipole.
Replacing one terminal chlorine in carbon tetrachloride by hydrogen breaks the
symmetry; chloroform has a nonzero molecular dipole.
Lone pairs can influence both geometry and the full charge distribution.
Ammonia and nitrogen trifluoride are both pyramidal, but their molecular
dipoles differ because the bond contributions align differently with the
overall electronic distribution.
Do not rank dipoles solely by central atom electronegativity or by counting
polar bonds.
For two equal dipole vectors separated by one hundred eighty degrees, the sum
is zero.
If the angle is smaller, the resultant generally is not zero.
Molecular dipole is an observable property of the complete charge
distribution;
individual bond arrows provide an approximate explanatory model.
Always establish the actual shape before claiming cancellation.
In valence bond language, head on overlap along the internuclear axis makes a
sigma bond, while side on overlap makes a pi bond.
An ordinary double bond has one sigma and one pi bond; a triple bond has one
sigma and two pi bonds.
Count every bond in the whole molecule, including those to hydrogen.
Ethene has four carbon hydrogen sigma bonds and one carbon carbon sigma bond,
plus one pi bond.
Its total is five sigma and one pi.
Each carbon is described by three sp two hybrid orbitals in a planar
arrangement, with an unhybridized p orbital forming the pi overlap.
Ethyne has two carbon hydrogen sigma bonds and one carbon carbon sigma bond,
plus two pi bonds.
Its total is three sigma and two pi.
Its carbons are described as sp hybridized and linear.
Methane is described using sp three hybrids in a tetrahedral arrangement.
Rotation that destroys a pi overlap is energetically restricted, unlike the
simplified picture of free rotation about an isolated sigma bond.
Hybridization is a localized model connecting orbital combinations with
bonding
patterns, not a directly measured label that independently proves every
molecular geometry.
Molecular orbitals extend across a molecule.
Compatible atomic wavefunctions combine into bonding and antibonding
combinations.
Fill these orbitals according to their energies, Pauli's limit and Hund's
rule.
Bond order is half the difference between bonding and antibonding electron
counts.
Hydrogen molecule has two bonding electrons and no antibonding electrons,
giving bond order one.
The elementary helium molecule configuration fills both corresponding orbitals
and has bond order zero, so that model predicts no ordinary stable covalent
helium dimer.
Weakly bound helium pairs involve physics beyond this simple bonding picture.
Oxygen has two unpaired electrons in degenerate pi antibonding orbitals,
explaining its paramagnetism.
Its bond order is two.
Removing one antibonding electron to make oxygen molecular cation raises bond
order to two point five and leaves one unpaired electron.
Adding one to make superoxide lowers bond order to one point five and leaves
one unpaired electron.
Adding two to make peroxide gives bond order one with the relevant electrons
paired.
Within this related series, greater bond order generally correlates with
shorter and stronger bonds.
Orbital energy ordering differs among diatomic molecules, so do not copy one
molecular orbital diagram blindly onto every species.
Hydrogen bonding requires an appropriate donor and acceptor.
In common introductory examples, a hydrogen bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or
fluorine interacts with a suitable lone pair on another electronegative atom.
Do not assume that every hydrogen atom or every lone pair is equally
effective.
Water can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds and forms an extended network.
This helps explain its unusually high boiling point relative to comparable
small hydrides and the open structure of ordinary ice.
Intermolecular hydrogen bonds link different molecules.
Intramolecular hydrogen bonds form within one molecule and may compete with
interactions with neighbours or solvent.
Compare ethanol and dimethyl ether: both have two carbons, six hydrogens and
one oxygen, but ethanol has an oxygen hydrogen donor while dimethyl ether does
not.
Ether can accept hydrogen bonds from water but cannot form the same self
associated donor network as ethanol.
Ethanol consequently has the higher normal boiling point.
Solubility and boiling point also depend on molecular size, shape, dispersion
forces and other interactions, so hydrogen bonding is not the only variable.
Use the twelve original questions to review electron counts, shapes, dipoles
and orbital models.
Further lattice cycles and complete molecular orbital diagrams remain useful
practice.
A Born Haber cycle relates formation of an ionic solid to a sequence of
gaseous
atom and ion steps.
Use the supplied illustrative sodium chloride data in kilojoules per mole:
sodium sublimation plus one hundred eight, sodium ionization plus four hundred
ninety six, half the chlorine bond dissociation plus one hundred twenty two,
and chlorine electron gain minus three hundred forty nine.
Suppose solid formation from the elements is minus four hundred eleven.
The nonlattice steps sum to plus three hundred seventy seven, so lattice
formation must be minus seven hundred eighty eight to close the cycle.
This is the enthalpy for gaseous sodium and chloride ions forming solid sodium
chloride.
Reversing that process gives lattice dissociation plus seven hundred eighty
eight.
Some tables use the opposite lattice convention, so copy the defining reaction
before the sign.
The chlorine contribution is half a mole of diatomic molecules for one mole of
salt; using the full dissociation value would double that step incorrectly.
The cycle uses Hess's law, not a new independent empirical sign rule.
Check both the balanced overall reaction and the physical states of every
intermediate.
Removing an electron does not always strengthen a chemical bond.
The result depends on whether that electron occupied a bonding or an
antibonding molecular orbital.
In the elementary nitrogen molecule diagram, nitrogen has bond order three and
its highest occupied orbital is a sigma bonding orbital.
Removing one electron to form the nitrogen molecular cation lowers bond order
to two point five and leaves an unpaired electron.
Oxygen starts with bond order two and two unpaired electrons in the degenerate
pi antibonding set.
Removing one of those antibonding electrons raises bond order to two point
five
and leaves one unpaired electron.
Thus the same operation, ionization, produces opposite bond order changes in
these two examples.
Their equal final bond orders do not prove identical bond lengths or bond
energies, because the atoms and orbital energies differ.
For a given related molecular series, bond order often helps compare length
and
strength, but it is not a universal numerical conversion between different
elements.
State the appropriate orbital energy ordering, locate the electron being
removed, and then recount bonding, antibonding and unpaired electrons before
assigning stability or magnetism.
Molecular shape describes the positions of atoms, while electron domain
geometry includes lone pairs.
Sulfur tetrafluoride has four bonding domains and one lone pair in the
elementary valence shell model.
Five domains adopt a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement.
Placing the lone pair in an equatorial site reduces the number of ninety
degree
interactions, leaving a seesaw arrangement of atoms.
Chlorine trifluoride has three bonds and two lone pairs, again five domains.
The two lone pairs preferentially occupy equatorial sites, leaving a T shaped
atomic arrangement.
Xenon tetrafluoride instead has six domains: four bonds and two lone pairs.
An octahedral domain arrangement with the lone pairs opposite each other
leaves
four fluorine atoms in one square plane.
All three molecules have different domain and atomic descriptions; counting
bonds alone cannot distinguish them.
These are qualitative valence shell geometries, and actual bond angles can
deviate from ideal drawings.
Use a valid electron count and molecular charge before assigning the number of
lone pairs.
A drawing should label lone pairs separately from atoms so an electron domain
diagram is not mistaken for the observed molecular shape.
Resonance contributors represent one delocalized electronic structure, not
molecules rapidly switching between different drawings.
In nitrate, three equivalent oxygen positions can share the double bond in the
simplest equivalent Lewis contributors.
Each contributor has one double and two single nitrogen oxygen bonds, so the
total Lewis bond order across those three links is four.
The average for each equivalent link is four thirds.
In nitrite, the two equivalent oxygen positions share one single and one
double
link in the elementary contributors, giving average one point five.
These bookkeeping averages are useful descriptions, not a promise that bond
order is always an exactly measured fractional observable.
Equivalent atom positions and contributor weights matter.
For unequally weighted contributors, taking a simple unweighted average can
mislead.
Also keep the overall ionic charge fixed while moving electrons; resonance
does
not move the nuclei or create a different atom connectivity.
Formal charges in individual nitrate contributors add to minus one even though
their distribution changes.
Compare equivalent bonds within the same species and distinguish an average
resonance representation from assigning one permanently short double bond and
separate permanently long single bonds.
A molecular dipole is a vector sum, so equal bond dipoles do not automatically
cancel.
Consider a simple two bond model in which the vectors have equal magnitude mu
and included angle theta.
Adding their components along the angle bisector gives resultant two times mu
times the cosine of half theta.
At one hundred eighty degrees, the equal opposing vectors cancel.
At one hundred twenty degrees, cosine sixty is one half, so the resultant
equals one bond dipole rather than zero.
At ninety degrees, the magnitude is square root two times mu.
These comparisons use the specified vector model; they are not an exact method
for predicting every molecule's measured dipole moment from an isolated bond
table.
Lone pairs and the full electron distribution can affect real molecular
values.
A symmetric molecule with several bonds may cancel all vector components, but
the actual geometry and identities must support that cancellation.
Draw arrows consistently and specify whether a chemistry dipole arrow or the
physical electric dipole vector convention is being used.
Reversing all arrows together preserves the calculated magnitude, while
reversing just one changes the model.
A Born Haber cycle for a divalent metal chloride must account for the full
ionic formula.
Use supplied illustrative energy terms for forming one mole of magnesium
chloride solid from magnesium solid and chlorine gas.
Magnesium atomization is plus one hundred forty eight kilojoules per mole, the
first and second magnesium ionizations are plus seven hundred thirty eight and
plus fourteen hundred fifty one, and converting one chlorine molecule into two
gas atoms costs plus two hundred forty three.
Each chlorine atom gains one electron with energy change minus three hundred
forty nine, so that term occurs twice.
These steps before lattice formation sum to plus eighteen hundred eighty two
kilojoules per mole.
If the supplied overall formation enthalpy is minus six hundred forty two, the
lattice formation enthalpy is minus twenty five hundred twenty four kilojoules
per mole.
The corresponding lattice dissociation value has the opposite sign for the
same
states.
Using only the first magnesium ionization would leave the metal charge wrong.
Using only one chlorine electron gain would fail the formula count.
Label initial and final states and write the energy equation before solving
for
the missing term.
A small change in ionic charge can change both electron count and molecular
shape.
For the nitrite ion, nitrogen contributes five valence electrons, two oxygens
contribute twelve, and the negative charge adds one, giving eighteen.
In the ordinary octet Lewis description, nitrogen has two oxygen neighbours
and
one lone pair.
One double and one single bond can be drawn in either of two equivalent
resonance contributors.
Three electron domains around nitrogen give a bent molecular shape, while
resonance makes the equivalent oxygen positions share the bonding description.
The nitronium ion has the same atom count but two fewer electrons because its
charge is positive rather than negative.
Sixteen valence electrons support the familiar two double bond Lewis
arrangement with no central nitrogen lone pair.
Two electron domains give a linear molecular shape.
A double bond counts as one domain for this purpose.
Do not confuse either closed shell ion with neutral nitrogen dioxide, which
has
seventeen valence electrons and an odd electron.
Count charge before applying a memorized shape or copying a Lewis diagram.
Geometry follows the relevant electronic description, not the atom formula
with
the charge silently omitted.
Average bond enthalpies estimate reaction energy by breaking gas phase
reactant
bonds and forming gas phase product bonds.
Consider ethene plus hydrogen giving ethane.
Use supplied average values in kilojoules per mole: carbon carbon double bond
six hundred fourteen, hydrogen hydrogen four hundred thirty six, carbon carbon
single bond three hundred forty seven, and carbon hydrogen four hundred
thirteen.
Four carbon hydrogen bonds occur on each side and cancel from a net
bookkeeping
list.
The changed bond set breaks one carbon carbon double bond and one hydrogen
hydrogen bond, costing ten hundred fifty kilojoules per mole.
It forms one carbon carbon single bond and two additional carbon hydrogen
bonds, releasing eleven hundred seventy three.
The estimated net is minus one hundred twenty three kilojoules per mole.
Forgetting the retained sigma bond in the product or subtracting all product
energy with the wrong sign changes the result.
Average bond values depend on molecular environment and do not make this an
exact enthalpy of hydrogenation.
Liquid and solid phase changes need separate terms if the reaction states
differ from the gas phase model.
State the bond inventory and the approximation before interpreting the sign.
Different atoms in a diatomic molecule require more care than copying every
feature of a homonuclear orbital diagram.
Carbon monoxide has ten valence electrons, while nitric oxide has eleven.
In the introductory molecular orbital counting model, carbon monoxide has bond
order three and all electrons paired.
Nitric oxide has one electron in an antibonding pi orbital, giving bond order
two point five and one unpaired electron.
It is therefore paramagnetic in this elementary comparison.
Removing that antibonding electron from nitric oxide gives the nitrosonium
ion,
with ten valence electrons, bond order three and a paired configuration in the
same model.
The general counting expression is one half the bonding minus antibonding
electron populations.
However, heteronuclear atomic orbitals begin at unequal energies, and the
resulting molecular orbitals need not have equal contributions on both atoms.
Electron count alone therefore does not prove equal dipole moments, identical
orbital energies or identical bond lengths for different molecules.
This chapter supplies an introductory population comparison, not a complete
heteronuclear orbital derivation.
Use the stated filling model and identify the orbital from which an electron
is
removed rather than assuming every ionization weakens every bond.
The relative order of sigma and pi molecular orbitals is not identical for
every second period diatomic molecule.
In the introductory valence orbital diagram for boron two, carbon two and
nitrogen two, the bonding pi two p pair lies below the bonding sigma two p
orbital.
The filled sigma two s and sigma star two s orbitals contribute equal bonding
and antibonding populations, cancelling in the bond order.
Boron two has six valence electrons.
Its final two occupy the two degenerate bonding pi orbitals singly with
parallel spins, giving bond order one and two unpaired electrons.
It is paramagnetic in this model.
Carbon two has eight valence electrons and fills both pi orbitals, giving bond
order two with all electrons paired.
Nitrogen two adds two electrons to the bonding sigma two p orbital, giving
bond
order three and a paired configuration.
Filled core orbitals have been omitted because their bonding contributions
cancel here.
Do not transfer the oxygen two orbital ordering unchanged to these three
molecules.
Use the appropriate energy order, Pauli exclusion and Hund's rule together
before assigning bond order or magnetism.
A coordinate bond describes the origin of an electron pair in a bond forming
step.
Ammonia has a nitrogen lone pair and can act as a Lewis base.
In the simple Lewis structure of boron trifluoride, boron has only six
electrons around it and can accept a pair as a Lewis acid.
Donation from nitrogen to boron gives the ammonia boron trifluoride adduct.
The donor arrow points from nitrogen toward boron; it does not represent a
proton transfer.
In the resulting single bond Lewis drawing, nitrogen has four bonds and no
lone
pair, so its formal charge is five minus four, or plus one.
Boron also has four bonds, giving three minus four, or minus one.
The total adduct remains neutral.
These formal charges are electron bookkeeping, not proof of complete ionic
separation or measured atomic charges.
Around each bonded nitrogen and boron centre there are four bond domains,
approximately tetrahedral rather than the original trigonal planar boron
arrangement.
No new electrons were created: the nitrogen pair became shared.
After formation, the bond is a shared electron pair interaction, not a
separate
physical class exempt from ordinary bonding principles.
Hydrogen bonding can link molecules or connect suitable sites within one
molecule.
In two nitrophenol, the hydroxyl group and neighbouring nitro group can form
an
intramolecular hydrogen bond from the hydroxyl hydrogen to a nitro oxygen.
The nearby positions permit a favourable internal arrangement.
In four nitrophenol, the para positions do not allow that same local
connection, and intermolecular hydrogen bonding becomes important.
The difference affects association between molecules and helps explain why the
ortho isomer is more steam volatile in the familiar separation comparison.
This does not mean that an internally hydrogen bonded molecule has no
interactions with water or with other molecules.
Nor does one hydrogen bond label uniquely determine every solubility or
melting
point.
Crystal packing, molecular shape, solvent and temperature also matter.
Identify the donor and acceptor explicitly: a hydroxyl group supplies the
donor
hydrogen, while a suitable nitro oxygen acts as acceptor.
The nitro group contains no nitrogen hydrogen donor simply because nitrogen is
present.
Compare the geometry and competing interactions before turning a structural
observation into a physical property prediction.
A reliable sigma and pi count begins with the molecular connectivity.
Every bonded atom pair has one sigma connection in the elementary localized
description.
A double bond contributes one additional pi bond and a triple bond contributes
two.
Ethyne has two carbon hydrogen sigma bonds and one carbon carbon sigma bond,
giving three sigma and two pi bonds altogether.
Now read the structure of acrylonitrile as a carbon bearing two hydrogens,
double bonded to a carbon bearing one hydrogen, then single bonded to a carbon
which is triple bonded to nitrogen.
There are three carbon hydrogen connections and three connections along the
heavy atom chain, giving six sigma bonds.
The carbon carbon double bond supplies one pi bond and the nitrile supplies
two, for three pi bonds.
In benzene, six ring connections and six carbon hydrogen bonds give twelve
sigma bonds.
A drawing with alternating single and double bonds contains three formal pi
bonds, but the actual six pi electrons are delocalized over the ring rather
than confined permanently to three selected links.
Count implicit hydrogens and distinguish an electron count from a bond count.
A structural drawing is essential; molecular formula alone need not determine
the arrangement of all bonds.
A heteronuclear molecular orbital diagram must respect orbital symmetry and
unequal atomic energies.
Take the hydrogen fluoride bond as the z axis.
In a supplied simplified valence model, hydrogen one s interacts most usefully
with fluorine two p z to form a sigma bonding and a sigma antibonding orbital.
The perpendicular fluorine two p x and two p y orbitals have the wrong
symmetry
for this overlap with hydrogen one s and are treated as nonbonding.
The much deeper fluorine two s level is also treated as largely nonbonding in
this introductory model.
Hydrogen contributes one valence electron and fluorine seven.
Place two in the low fluorine two s derived level, two in the sigma bond and
four across the two perpendicular nonbonding orbitals.
Sigma star remains empty.
The bonding minus antibonding count divided by two gives bond order one, and
every occupied orbital is paired, consistent with diamagnetism.
The occupied molecular orbitals need not contain equal hydrogen and fluorine
contributions.
The diagram is qualitative and omits core electrons and detailed mixing;
homonuclear gerade and ungerade labels do not apply to this unequal atom
molecule.
A bond potential curve measures energy against internuclear separation, rather
than plotting a reaction rate.
Choose separated ground state atoms as zero potential energy.
At very short distance, strong repulsion raises the curve; attraction lowers
it
toward a minimum at the equilibrium separation.
At that minimum the slope is zero, so the net force is zero.
This does not mean that separating the atoms costs no energy.
The vertical depth from the minimum to separated atoms is called D e.
A supporting quantum refinement recognizes that the lowest vibrational level
lies above the minimum by its zero point energy.
Dissociation from that level therefore requires D zero, equal to D e minus the
zero point contribution.
For illustrative values of four hundred fifty kilojoules per mole for the well
depth and twenty five for the zero point energy, D zero is four hundred twenty
five kilojoules per mole.
These are supplied model values, not a measured bond assignment or an average
bond enthalpy at an unspecified temperature.
On the long distance side of the minimum the force attracts the atoms back; on
the short distance side it pushes them apart.
Insert neutral nitrogen dioxide between the familiar nitronium and nitrite
ions.
Nitrogen contributes five valence electrons and two oxygens contribute twelve.
Removing one electron gives sixteen for nitronium, leaving seventeen for
neutral nitrogen dioxide and adding one gives eighteen for nitrite.
The isolated neutral molecule therefore cannot have every electron paired.
Its ground state is a bent radical and is paramagnetic.
Nitronium is linear in the ordinary closed shell model, whereas nitrite is
bent
with a central lone pair.
Do not assign the neutral radical a closed shell electron pair picture merely
because it shares the same atom skeleton.
Nor does a one electron change simply mean that one complete bond disappears.
Two nitrogen dioxide radicals can combine to form dinitrogen tetroxide, whose
usual ground state has paired electrons.
Their gas mixture is an equilibrium composition that depends on temperature
and
pressure, so a sample's magnetic or colour observation need not correspond to
pure isolated nitrogen dioxide molecules alone.
Counting an odd number establishes at least one unpaired electron; it does not
by itself determine the exact bond angle or every detail of the molecular
orbital diagram.
A positional isomer comparison tests whether a vector rule survives a change
in geometry.
Use an explicitly idealized planar regular benzene ring with two equal outward
radial carbon chlorine bond dipoles, and neglect other dipole contributions.
Adjacent ortho substitution puts the two vectors sixty degrees apart, meta
substitution gives one hundred twenty degrees, and opposite para substitution
gives one hundred eighty degrees.
The magnitude of their sum is twice the individual magnitude times the
absolute
cosine of half their angle.
The predicted magnitudes are square root three times mu, mu, and zero,
respectively.
For an illustrative individual contribution of one point five zero debye, the
model gives approximately two point six zero, one point five zero, and zero
debye.
Equal chemical bonds cancel only when their vectors oppose with matching
magnitudes; their equality alone is insufficient.
Para symmetry supports cancellation for the symmetric molecule, but the
numerical ortho and meta estimates are model outputs, not guaranteed measured
dipole moments.
Real electron redistribution and geometry can modify local bond contributions.
Changing one substituent also removes the equal vector assumption, so opposite
placement by itself no longer guarantees cancellation.
